claim: LRRK2 is a Parkinson's disease (PD)-linked protein consisting of seven domains, including a kinase and a Roc G domain.
source: The Parkinson's disease (PD)-linked protein Leucine-Rich Repeat Kinase 2 (LRRK2) consists of seven domains, including a kinase and a Roc G domain.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a basic characterization of LRRK2 structure.

claim: LRRK2 has a KM value that lies within the range of the physiological GTP concentrations within the cell.
source: By in-depth biochemical analysis, assessing the Michaelis–Menten kinetics of the Roc G domain, we have confirmed that LRRK2 has, similar to other Roco protein family members, a KM value of LRRK2 that lies within the range of the physiological GTP concentrations within the cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental Michaelis-Menten kinetics data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The R1441G PD variant located within the Roc domain showed an increased catalytic efficiency.
source: Furthermore, the R1441G PD variant located within a mutational hotspot in the Roc domain showed an increased catalytic efficiency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental kinetic measurements comparing R1441G to wild-type LRRK2.

claim: The G2019S PD variant, located in the kinase domain, showed an increased KM and reduced catalytic efficiency.
source: In contrast, the most common PD variant G2019S, located in the kinase domain, showed an increased KM and reduced catalytic efficiency, suggesting a negative feedback mechanism from the kinase domain to the G domain.
evidence: This is supported by experimental kinetic measurements and suggests a mechanistic interpretation.

claim: Autophosphorylation of the G1+2 residue (T1343) in the Roc P-loop motif is critical for phosphoregulation of both the KM and the kcat values of the Roc-catalyzed GTP hydrolysis.
source: Autophosphorylation of the G1+2 residue (T1343) in the Roc P-loop motif is critical for this phosphoregulation of both the KM and the kcat values of the Roc-catalyzed GTP hydrolysis, most likely by changing the monomer–dimer equilibrium.
evidence: This is supported by mutational analysis and kinetic measurements of T1343A variant.

claim: The LRRK2 T1343A variant has a similar increased kinase activity in cells compared to G2019S.
source: The LRRK2 T1343A variant has a similar increased kinase activity in cells compared to G2019S and the double mutant T1343A/G2019S has no further increased activity, suggesting that T1343 is crucial for the negative feedback in the LRRK2 signaling cascade.
evidence: This is supported by cell-based Rab10 phosphorylation assays.

claim: The double mutant T1343A/G2019S has no further increased activity compared to T1343A alone.
source: The LRRK2 T1343A variant has a similar increased kinase activity in cells compared to G2019S and the double mutant T1343A/G2019S has no further increased activity, suggesting that T1343 is crucial for the negative feedback in the LRRK2 signaling cascade.
evidence: This is supported by cell-based Rab10 phosphorylation assays comparing single and double mutants.

claim: T1343 is crucial for the negative feedback in the LRRK2 signaling cascade.
source: The LRRK2 T1343A variant has a similar increased kinase activity in cells compared to G2019S and the double mutant T1343A/G2019S has no further increased activity, suggesting that T1343 is crucial for the negative feedback in the LRRK2 signaling cascade.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that T1343A mutation phenocopies G2019S and the double mutant shows no additive effect.

claim: PD mutants differently change the kinetics of the GTPase cycle, which might in part explain the difference in penetrance of these mutations in PD patients.
source: Interestingly, PD mutants differently change the kinetics of the GTPase cycle, which might in part explain the difference in penetrance of these mutations in PD patients.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the kinetic data in relation to clinical observations.

claim: Nonsynonymous sequence variants within LRRK2 are associated with familial forms of Parkinson's disease.
source: Nonsynonymous sequence variants within the Leucine-Rich Repeat Kinase 2 (LRRK2) are associated with familial forms of Parkinson's disease (PD) and are phenotypically indistinguishable from idiopathic forms of PD (iPD) (Paisán-Ruíz et al., 2004; Zimprich et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: LRRK2-associated familial PD is phenotypically indistinguishable from idiopathic forms of PD.
source: Nonsynonymous sequence variants within the Leucine-Rich Repeat Kinase 2 (LRRK2) are associated with familial forms of Parkinson's disease (PD) and are phenotypically indistinguishable from idiopathic forms of PD (iPD) (Paisán-Ruíz et al., 2004; Zimprich et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The LRRK2 locus contributes to an increased risk of developing idiopathic PD.
source: In addition to defined pathogenic as well as PD-risk coding variants, the LRRK2 locus also contributes to an increased risk of developing iPD more generally, as shown in genome-wide association studies (Simón-Sánchez et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to genome-wide association studies.

claim: LRRK2 is a multidomain protein which belongs to the Roco protein family.
source: LRRK2 is a multidomain protein, which belongs to the Roco protein family (Marín et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: LRRK2 contains a core module conserved among Roco proteins, consisting of a Roc G domain and a COR dimerization domain, followed by a kinase domain.
source: Besides a core module, conserved among the Roco proteins, consisting of a Roc (Ras of complex proteins) G domain and a COR (C-terminal of Roc) dimerization domain, which is followed by a kinase domain, it contains four predicted solenoid domains.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about LRRK2.

claim: LRRK2 contains four predicted solenoid domains.
source: Besides a core module, conserved among the Roco proteins, consisting of a Roc (Ras of complex proteins) G domain and a COR (C-terminal of Roc) dimerization domain, which is followed by a kinase domain, it contains four predicted solenoid domains.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about LRRK2.

claim: The three N-terminal solenoid domains of LRRK2 consist of Armadillo repeats followed by an Ankyrin domain and leucine-rich repeats.
source: The three N-terminal solenoid domains consist of Armadillo repeats followed by an Ankyrin domain and the namesake leucine-rich repeats, while the C-terminus is formed by a seven-bladed WD40 domain (Mills et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The C-terminus of LRRK2 is formed by a seven-bladed WD40 domain.
source: The three N-terminal solenoid domains consist of Armadillo repeats followed by an Ankyrin domain and the namesake leucine-rich repeats, while the C-terminus is formed by a seven-bladed WD40 domain (Mills et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The solenoid domains of LRRK2 are involved in protein-protein interactions.
source: By similarity, these domains are involved in protein–protein interactions and, based on recent structural models and high-resolution structures, are likely to be involved in the intramolecular regulation of the protein, as well as, for example, by keeping the kinase domain in an auto-inhibited state (Deniston et al., 2020; Gloeckner and Porras, 2020; Guaitoli et al., 2016; Taylor et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from structural similarity and supported by citations.

claim: The solenoid domains of LRRK2 are likely involved in intramolecular regulation of the protein.
source: By similarity, these domains are involved in protein–protein interactions and, based on recent structural models and high-resolution structures, are likely to be involved in the intramolecular regulation of the protein, as well as, for example, by keeping the kinase domain in an auto-inhibited state (Deniston et al., 2020; Gloeckner and Porras, 2020; Guaitoli et al., 2016; Taylor et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from structural models and high-resolution structures cited.

claim: The solenoid domains of LRRK2 keep the kinase domain in an auto-inhibited state.
source: By similarity, these domains are involved in protein–protein interactions and, based on recent structural models and high-resolution structures, are likely to be involved in the intramolecular regulation of the protein, as well as, for example, by keeping the kinase domain in an auto-inhibited state (Deniston et al., 2020; Gloeckner and Porras, 2020; Guaitoli et al., 2016; Taylor et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from structural models and high-resolution structures cited.

claim: Membrane-bound LRRK2 phosphorylates a specific set of Rab proteins at a conserved threonine residue within their switch II motif.
source: Moreover, membrane-bound LRRK2 has been demonstrated to phosphorylate a specific set of Rab proteins at a conserved threonine residue within their switch II motif, including Rab8a and Rab10 (Gomez et al., 2019; Steger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: LRRK2 phosphorylates Rab8a and Rab10.
source: Moreover, membrane-bound LRRK2 has been demonstrated to phosphorylate a specific set of Rab proteins at a conserved threonine residue within their switch II motif, including Rab8a and Rab10 (Gomez et al., 2019; Steger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: LRRK2 kinase activity is involved in endo-lysosomal pathways.
source: In addition, LRRK2 kinase activity has been demonstrated to be involved in endo-lysosomal pathways, thereby being a regulator of the innate immunity (Ahmadi Rastegar and Dzamko, 2020; Bonet-Ponce and Cookson, 2019; Erb and Moore, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: LRRK2 is a regulator of innate immunity.
source: In addition, LRRK2 kinase activity has been demonstrated to be involved in endo-lysosomal pathways, thereby being a regulator of the innate immunity (Ahmadi Rastegar and Dzamko, 2020; Bonet-Ponce and Cookson, 2019; Erb and Moore, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The kinase activity of LRRK2 is dependent on the guanine nucleotide-binding capacity of the Roc domain.
source: It is clear that the kinase activity of LRRK2 is dependent on the guanine nucleotide-binding capacity of the Roc domain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The nucleotide state of the Roc domain has been suggested to regulate dimerization in a bacterial Roco protein.
source: Previous work on the conserved RocCOR module of a bacterial Roco protein has suggested that the nucleotide state of the Roc domain regulates dimerization (Deyaert et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on bacterial Roco proteins.

claim: A monomer-dimer/oligomer transition plays a critical role in LRRK2 protein activation.
source: Consistently, also accumulating data shows that a monomer dimer/oligomer transition plays a critical role in LRRK2 protein activation (Berger et al., 2010; Schapansky et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: LRRK2 shuttles between a monomeric cytosolic state and kinase-active oligomeric forms localized at the membrane.
source: Cellular data suggest that LRRK2 shuttles between a monomeric cytosolic states and kinase-active oligomeric forms localized at the membrane (Berger et al., 2010; James et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cellular studies.

claim: Rab29-induced tetramerization represents the kinase active state of LRRK2.
source: Further support comes from recent high-resolution structures, indicating that a Rab29-induced tetramerization represents the kinase active state (Wu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural studies.

claim: Autophosphorylation induces LRRK2 monomerization.
source: Our recent data revealed that autophosphorylation induces LRRK2 monomerization (Guaitoli et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' recent work.

claim: The Roc domain has been identified as a major target of LRRK2 autophosphorylation.
source: Interestingly, the Roc domain has been identified as a major target of LRRK2 autophosphorylation by phospho-proteomic analysis (Gloeckner et al., 2010; Greggio et al., 2009; Webber et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to phospho-proteomic studies.

claim: Autophosphorylation of the Roc G domain modifies GTP-binding activities.
source: Furthermore, there are indications that autophosphorylation of the Roc G domain modifies GTP-binding activities (Webber et al., 2011) and that trans-phosphorylation by the kinase domain of the LRRK2 orthologue Dictyostelium Roco4 enhances GTPase activity (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Trans-phosphorylation by the kinase domain of Dictyostelium Roco4 enhances GTPase activity.
source: Furthermore, there are indications that autophosphorylation of the Roc G domain modifies GTP-binding activities (Webber et al., 2011) and that trans-phosphorylation by the kinase domain of the LRRK2 orthologue Dictyostelium Roco4 enhances GTPase activity (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on Dictyostelium Roco4.

claim: LRRK2 has kinetic parameters comparable to other Roco protein family members.
source: LRRK2 has kinetic parameters comparable to other Roco protein family members.
evidence: This is stated based on comparison with previous studies on Roco proteins.

claim: The physiological GTP concentration within the cell is around 500 µM.
source: Strikingly, the KM value of LRRK2 lies within the range of the physiological GTP concentrations (around 500 µM; Traut, 1994) within the cell.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a reference on cellular GTP concentrations.

claim: Changes in global cellular or local GTP concentration might have a high impact on LRRK2 activity.
source: Therefore, changes in global cellular or local GTP concentration might have a high impact on protein activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that LRRK2's KM is near physiological GTP concentrations.

claim: R1441G, Y1699C, and G2019S are pathogenic LRRK2 variants with confirmed disease co-segregation.
source: For this reason, we here fully assessed the enzyme kinetics of disease-associated PD variants, in particular those with confirmed disease co-segregation. For this purpose, we selected three pathogenic variants, R1441G, localized within the Roc domain, the Y1699C variant in the COR-A domain, as well as the kinase-domain variant G2019S.
evidence: This is stated as the selection criteria for the study.

claim: R1441G, Y1699C, and G2019S variants significantly increase the phosphorylation of LRRK2 substrates Rab8a, Rab10, and Rab12.
source: All three variants significantly increase the phosphorylation of the LRRK2 substrates Rab8a, Rab10, and Rab12 (Kalogeropulou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: LRRK2 wt, R1441G, and Y1699C MBP-RocCOR constructs showed similar kinetic parameters in the charcoal assay.
source: LRRK2 wt, R1441G, as well as Y1699C MBP-RocCOR constructs showed similar kinetic parameters in the standard radiolabeling assay (charcoal assay), which determines the release of free inorganic phosphate (Pi) (Kolch, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-D.

claim: The catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) was identical for LRRK2 wt, R1441G, and Y1699C MBP-RocCOR constructs.
source: While slight differences were observed in the individual KM as well as kcat values, the catalytic efficiency determined by kcat/KM was identical (Figure 1A–D; Supplementary file 1a and b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The HPLC-based assay and charcoal assay result in comparable GTP hydrolysis rates for full-length LRRK2.
source: To ensure that both assays result in comparable results, we compared GTP hydrolysis rates (kobs) of full-length LRRK2 wt in both assays at two different GTP concentrations. Both assays, the HPLC-based assay as well as the charcoal assay, resulted in overall comparable kinetics, ensuring that the results of both assays can be directly compared (Figure 1E and F, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental comparison shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Wild-type full-length LRRK2 has a kcat of 0.36 ± 0.02 min–1 and a KM of 554 ± 62 µM.
source: For the wild-type full-length LRRK2 protein, we have determined a kcat of 0.36 ± 0.02 min–1 and a KM of 554 ± 62 µM confirming our previously published data, thus demonstrating the robustness of the used HPLC-based assay (Wauters et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental kinetic measurements and confirms previous published data.

claim: Full-length LRRK2 R1441G has a decreased KM (271 ± 27 µM) compared to wild-type.
source: Interestingly, full-length LRRK2 bearing the R1441G variant showed a decreased Michaelis–Menten constant (KM = 271 ± 27 µM) while the kcat increased compared to the wt (Figure 2A), leading to an augmented catalytic efficiency of that variant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental kinetic measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Full-length LRRK2 R1441G has an increased kcat compared to wild-type.
source: Interestingly, full-length LRRK2 bearing the R1441G variant showed a decreased Michaelis–Menten constant (KM = 271 ± 27 µM) while the kcat increased compared to the wt (Figure 2A), leading to an augmented catalytic efficiency of that variant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental kinetic measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Full-length LRRK2 G2019S has a significantly increased KM value of 867 ± 110 µM compared to wild-type (554 ± 62 µM).
source: In contrast, full-length G2019S LRRK2 showed a significantly increased KM value of 867 ± 110 µM compared to a wt reference (554 ± 62 µM), while no significant change in the kcat parameter (kcat = 0.36 min–1) was observed (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental kinetic measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Full-length LRRK2 G2019S shows no significant change in kcat compared to wild-type.
source: In contrast, full-length G2019S LRRK2 showed a significantly increased KM value of 867 ± 110 µM compared to a wt reference (554 ± 62 µM), while no significant change in the kcat parameter (kcat = 0.36 min–1) was observed (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental kinetic measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The kinase-dead K1906M LRRK2 variant has a KM value (181 ± 58 µM) approximately three times lower compared to wild-type LRRK2.
source: In fact, the KM value (KM = 181 ± 58 µM) for a K1906M kinase-dead LRRK2 variant is approximately three times lower compared to wt LRRK2 while the kcat value was only slightly reduced (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental kinetic measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The kinase-dead K1906M LRRK2 variant has a slightly reduced kcat compared to wild-type.
source: In fact, the KM value (KM = 181 ± 58 µM) for a K1906M kinase-dead LRRK2 variant is approximately three times lower compared to wt LRRK2 while the kcat value was only slightly reduced (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental kinetic measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MLi-2 treated full-length wild-type LRRK2 has a lower KM value.
source: Consistently, MLi-2 treated fl. wt LRRK2 also has a lower KM value (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which also ensures that the GTPase and not the kinase domain is the driver of the GTP consumption in our experimental setup (Liu and West, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The GTPase domain and not the kinase domain is the driver of GTP consumption in the experimental setup.
source: Consistently, MLi-2 treated fl. wt LRRK2 also has a lower KM value (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which also ensures that the GTPase and not the kinase domain is the driver of the GTP consumption in our experimental setup (Liu and West, 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the MLi-2 treatment experiment and supported by citation.

claim: An active kinase conformation provides a negative feedback signal on the Roc domain, most likely mediated via autophosphorylation.
source: This strongly suggests a negative feedback signal on the Roc domain conferred by an active kinase conformation, most likely mediated via autophosphorylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinase-dead mutant data showing opposite effects to G2019S.

claim: Incubation of wild-type LRRK2 with ATP for 2 hr at 30°C leads to an approximately twofold increase in KM (1036 ± 168 µM).
source: In fact, an incubation of the full-length wild-type protein with ATP for 2 hr at 30°C prior to determining its GTPase activity leads to altered Michaelis–Menten parameters, impacting the KM as well as kcat values. An approximately twofold increase in KM (1036 ± 168 µM) and an approximately twofold decrease in kcat (0.13 ± 0.01 min–1) demonstrate a strong reduction in LRRK2 GTPase activity by enforced autophosphorylation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Incubation of wild-type LRRK2 with ATP for 2 hr at 30°C leads to an approximately twofold decrease in kcat (0.13 ± 0.01 min–1).
source: In fact, an incubation of the full-length wild-type protein with ATP for 2 hr at 30°C prior to determining its GTPase activity leads to altered Michaelis–Menten parameters, impacting the KM as well as kcat values. An approximately twofold increase in KM (1036 ± 168 µM) and an approximately twofold decrease in kcat (0.13 ± 0.01 min–1) demonstrate a strong reduction in LRRK2 GTPase activity by enforced autophosphorylation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Incubation of the kinase-dead K1906M variant with ATP results in no significant change in KM and kcat values.
source: As a control condition, to rule out inactivation of the LRRK2 protein by degradation during pre-incubation, we incubated a dead variant (K1906M) with ATP, the same way as the wild-type, resulting in no significant change in KM and kcat values.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data serving as a control.

claim: Autophosphorylation negatively regulates the GTPase activity of LRRK2.
source: This shows that autophosphorylation indeed negatively regulates the GTPase activity of LRRK2.
evidence: This is concluded from the ATP incubation experiments comparing wild-type and kinase-dead variants.

claim: T1343 has been mapped as a phosphosite by phosphoproteomic studies.
source: T1343 has initially been mapped by phosphoproteomic studies (Gloeckner et al., 2010; Greggio et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to phosphoproteomic studies.

claim: T1343 is quantitatively phosphorylated in the C-terminal four-domain 'RCKW' construct.
source: Furthermore, it has been shown to be quantitatively phosphorylated in the C-terminal four-domain 'RCKW' construct, allowing resolving the phospho-threonine in the recently published cryo-EM structure (Deniston et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a cryo-EM structure study.

claim: T1343A showed no increase in KM value after ATP treatment.
source: In fact, T1343A showed no increase in KM value after ATP treatment, suggesting that this is the regulatory site which is crucial for the feedback mechanism (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: T1343A has a reduced kcat value compared to wild-type.
source: In addition to the lower KM value compared to wild-type that remains unaffected upon ATP treatment, also a reduced kcat value was observed for the T1343A mutant, which might suggest that the mutation is not completely structurally neutral.
evidence: This is supported by experimental kinetic measurements.

claim: The T1343A mutant does not result in unstable or aggregated protein.
source: However, the T1343A mutant does not result in instable or aggregated protein (see below) and, importantly, the T1343A mutant in the RocCOR domain is the only construct that does not significantly affect the GTPase activity (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations.

claim: The T1343A mutant in the RocCOR domain is the only construct that does not significantly affect the GTPase activity.
source: However, the T1343A mutant does not result in instable or aggregated protein (see below) and, importantly, the T1343A mutant in the RocCOR domain is the only construct that does not significantly affect the GTPase activity (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Supplementary file 1c.

claim: For the bacterium Chlorobium tepidum Roco protein, dimerization has been demonstrated to modulate GTPase activity.
source: Furthermore, for the Roco protein found in the bacterium Chlorobium tepidum, dimerization has been demonstrated to modulate GTPase activity (Deyaert et al., 2017; Gotthardt et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on bacterial Roco proteins.

claim: LRRK2 dimerization is impacted by LRRK2 autophosphorylation.
source: In fact, in a recent work we could demonstrate that LRRK2 dimerization is impacted by LRRK2 autophosphorylation (Guaitoli et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' recent work.

claim: Autophosphorylation shifts the monomer/dimer equilibrium toward the monomeric form.
source: In this work, we could demonstrate that autophosphorylation is shifting the monomer/dimer (m/d) equilibrium toward the monomeric form.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' recent work.

claim: For wild-type LRRK2, the monomer/dimer equilibrium can be shifted toward the monomer by in vitro autophosphorylation.
source: In contrast to the wild-type, for which the m/d equilibrium could be shifted toward the monomer by in vitro autophosphorylation, ATP incubation does not affect the percentage of dimer for the T1343A variant of LRRK2 (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data shown in Figure 5.

claim: ATP incubation does not affect the percentage of dimer for the T1343A variant of LRRK2.
source: In contrast to the wild-type, for which the m/d equilibrium could be shifted toward the monomer by in vitro autophosphorylation, ATP incubation does not affect the percentage of dimer for the T1343A variant of LRRK2 (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The underlying mechanism of the negative feedback phosphorylation toward lower GTPase activity might be mediated by an increased monomerization of LRRK2.
source: This suggests that the underlying mechanism of the negative feedback phosphorylation toward lower GTPase activity might be mediated by an increased monomerization of LRRK2.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that T1343A does not show ATP-induced changes in dimer percentage.

claim: T1343A LRRK2 has specific kinase activity at a level comparable to wild-type LRRK2.
source: By this assay, we could clearly demonstrate that T1343A confers specific kinase activity at a level comparable to the LRRK2 wt, while G2019S was clearly more active (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro LRRKtide assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: G2019S LRRK2 is more active than wild-type in the LRRKtide assay.
source: By this assay, we could clearly demonstrate that T1343A confers specific kinase activity at a level comparable to the LRRK2 wt, while G2019S was clearly more active (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro LRRKtide assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: R1441G and I2020T PD mutations showed an approximately eightfold increase in Rab10 phosphorylation.
source: In agreement with published data (Kalogeropulou et al., 2022), the other PD mutations R1441G and I2020T showed an approximately eightfold increase in Rab10 phosphorylation (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is supported by cell-based assay data shown in Figure 6C and D and agrees with published data.

claim: The T1343A variant showed an approximately twofold increase in Rab10 phosphorylation, which is comparable with G2019S.
source: Interestingly, the T1343A variant showed an approximately twofold increase in activity, which is comparable with G2019S, while the double mutant T1343A/G2019S did not further increase Rab10 phosphorylation (Figure 6 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell-based assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The double mutant T1343A/G2019S did not further increase Rab10 phosphorylation compared to single mutants.
source: Interestingly, the T1343A variant showed an approximately twofold increase in activity, which is comparable with G2019S, while the double mutant T1343A/G2019S did not further increase Rab10 phosphorylation (Figure 6 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell-based assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The T1343A variant disrupts the negative feedback regulation in the LRRK2 signaling cascade in cells.
source: Together, our results suggest that T1343 is crucial for the negative feedback in the LRRK2 signaling cascade in cells and the mutation to alanine disrupts this regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell-based assay results showing T1343A has similar activity to G2019S.

claim: Kinases and G-proteins are often found within the same signaling cascade but never on the same protein except for Roco proteins.
source: Kinases and G-proteins are often found within the same signaling cascade, but with the exception of Roco proteins, never on the same protein.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about signaling proteins.

claim: MAP-kinase signaling networks often include a negative feedback loop allowing stable signal, context-specific fine-tuning, and shutdown of the system.
source: In addition, these pathways often include a negative feedback loop allowing a stable signal, a context-specific fine-tuning, as well as shutdown of the system (Birtwistle and Kolch, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review on MAP-kinase signaling.

claim: EphA2-mediated negative feedback inhibition of the Ras–PI3K–AKT module leads to cell cycle arrest.
source: For example, an EphA2-mediated negative feedback inhibition of the Ras–PI3K–AKT module leads to a cell cycle arrest (Menges and McCance, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on EphA2 signaling.

claim: Most previous studies on LRRK2 GTPase activity are based on single kobs values at GTP concentrations around or below the KM for full-length LRRK2.
source: Nevertheless, knowledge of the interplay between these two domains is still limited. In addition, observations by most of the studies are based on single kobs values at considerable low GTP concentrations around or below the KM for full-length LRRK2-mediated GTP hydrolysis and/or worked with truncated LRRK2 constructs (Liu et al., 2010; Wauters et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: The physiological impact of differences in KM values is expected to lead to strong perturbation of tightly regulated LRRK2 activity.
source: Given an average physiological GTP concentration of approximately 500 µM within cells (Traut, 1994), the physiological impact of the differences in the KM values reported in this study, in combination with a negative feedback loop, is expected to lead to a strong perturbation of the tightly regulated LRRK2 activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data in the context of physiological GTP concentrations.

claim: The increased catalytic efficiency of R1441G is in good agreement with the penetrance of R1441 variants.
source: In fact, when looking at the catalytic efficiency, it is striking that we found it to be increased for the R1441G variant located within a mutational hotspot of the Roc domain, also containing the PD variants R1441C, H, and S, which is in good agreement with the penetrance of these variants (Haugarvoll et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data and supported by citation to a study on penetrance.

claim: R1441G shows strong Rab phosphorylation in cells while the effect mediated by G2019S is considerably weaker.
source: This finding is also in well agreement with the different impact of these pathogenic variants on the Rab phosphorylation. While R1441G shows a strong Rab phosphorylation in cells, the effect mediated by G2019S is considerably weaker (Kalogeropulou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on Rab phosphorylation by LRRK2 variants.

claim: T1343A and T1343G variants have been tested in previous studies showing similar activity to wild-type LRRK2 at basal conditions.
source: T1343A and T1343G variants have already been tested in two previous studies, however, only at basal conditions and/or in vitro where similar activity was observed in comparison to wild-type LRRK2 (Biosa et al., 2013; Störmer et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Replacing T1343 by a non-phosphorylatable residue reduced P33 incorporation in phosphorylation assays by 50%.
source: Furthermore, replacing T1343 by a non-phosphorylatable residue reduced P33 incorporation in phosphorylation assays by 50% (Greggio et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The AlphaFold3 model suggests that the phosphate of pT1343 is oriented inward, thereby substituting the gamma phosphate.
source: Interestingly, the AF3 model suggests that the phosphate of the pT1343 is orientated inward, thereby substituting the gamma phosphate (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on AlphaFold3 modeling shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The AlphaFold3 model finding is in agreement with MD simulations published recently.
source: This finding is well in agreement with MD simulations published recently (Störmer et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent MD simulation study.

claim: pT1343 might hamper GTP hydrolysis by competing with GTP re-binding.
source: As we are determining GTP hydrolysis in a multi-turnover situation, the pT1343 might hamper the hydrolysis by competing with GTP re-binding.
evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation based on the structural model and experimental setup.

claim: Other Rab proteins are phosphorylated at a conserved serine or threonine residue at the homologous position within the P-loop.
source: Interestingly, according to phosphoproteomes curated in the PhosphoSitePlus database (https://www.phosphosite.org) also other Rabs are phosphorylated either at a conserved serine or threonine residue at the homologous position (G1+2) within the P-loop (for a P-loop alignment of all Rabs, see Mishra et al., 2013), including Rab1a, Rab5a, Rab7a, Rab8a, Rab10, Rab13, Rab15, Rab17, and Rab35, as well as Rab2 and Rab22a, respectively.
evidence: This is based on database information and supported by citation.

claim: Rab24 has a phosphorylatable tyrosine (Y17) at the P-loop position.
source: Furthermore, the atypical Rab protein Rab24 has a phosphorylatable tyrosine (Y17) at this position (Ding et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on Rab24.

claim: Rab24 Y17A shows an increase in intrinsic GTP hydrolysis rate.
source: In agreement with the findings for LRRK2 described here, Rab24 Y17A shows an increase in intrinsic GTP hydrolysis rate (Wu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on Rab24.

claim: P-loop phosphorylation is a relevant and conserved regulatory mechanism for Rab proteins.
source: Together, these findings suggest that P-loop phosphorylation is a relevant and conserved regulatory mechanism for Rab proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations about P-loop phosphorylation in multiple Rab proteins.

claim: Increasing the GTP-loaded portion of LRRK2 favors its monomeric state, as shown for its bacterial ortholog.
source: As shown for its bacterial ortholog (Deyaert et al., 2017), increasing the GTP-loaded portion of LRRK2 favors its monomeric state.
evidence: This is inferred from studies on bacterial orthologs and supported by citation.

claim: GTP hydrolysis leads to a GDP-bound state of LRRK2, potentially inducing dimerization at a critical local protein concentration.
source: GTP hydrolysis leads, at least transiently, to a GDP-bound state of LRRK2, potentially inducing dimerization at a critical local protein concentration.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on the GTPase cycle and dimerization data.

claim: LRRK2 kinase activity might counteract dimerization by autophosphorylation of T1343, shifting the equilibrium back to the monomeric state.
source: LRRK2 kinase activity might counteract this mechanism by autophosphorylation of the P-loop residue T1343, shifting the equilibrium back to the monomeric state.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on the experimental data.

claim: The CtRoco dimer structure revealed a dimer-stabilized orientation of the P-loop that would prevent direct nucleotide binding on the dimer.
source: This hypothesis is supported by recently determined EM structures of the bacterial LRRK2 homolog ctRoco (Galicia et al., 2024). This CtRoco dimer structure revealed a dimer-stabilized orientation of the P-loop, which would prevent direct nucleotide binding on the dimer.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent EM structure study.

claim: The CtRoco structure supports a critical role of the P-loop conformation in nucleotide-induced monomerization.
source: This therefore further supports a critical role of the P-loop conformation in the nucleotide-induced monomerization.
evidence: This is inferred from the CtRoco structure and its implications.

claim: There is tight regulation between GTPase activity, phosphorylation, and monomer-dimer equilibrium that interplay to regulate LRRK2 signal output.
source: This suggests that there is a tight regulation between GTPase activity, phosphorylation, and monomer dimer equilibrium, which all interplay with each other to regulate the LRRK2 signal output.
evidence: This is inferred from the collective experimental observations.

claim: Compounds targeting either the kinase, G domain, or dimerization can block LRRK2 activity and signaling.
source: Consistently, compounds target either the kinase, G domain, or dimerization can block LRRK2 activity and signaling (Helton et al., 2021; Pathak et al., 2023; Wojewska and Kortholt, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on LRRK2 inhibitors.

claim: The kinase domain in its active conformation negatively regulates GTP hydrolysis, similar to MAPK pathways where negative feedback mechanisms are essential.
source: In conclusion, our study describes a novel intramolecular feedback mechanism of LRRK2, which is based on autophosphorylation. Similar to MAPK pathways where negative feedback mechanisms are essential to guarantee a robust signal, and also allowing a tight and context-specific shutdown of the pathway, the kinase domain in its active conformation negatively regulates GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, drawing an analogy to MAPK pathways.
